meta.framing: How do courts decide whether a person who performs services is an employee or an independent contractor when the written contract and the actual working relationship point in different directions, as in the litigation culminating in the UK Supreme Court's decision in Uber BV v Aslam?

response:
When a written contract and the lived reality of a working relationship point in different directions, an English court must decide which of them governs the classification of the person performing the services. The litigation brought by drivers against Uber brought that question into sharp relief. Uber argued that its drivers were independent contractors who contracted directly with passengers, and it relied on documentation carefully drafted to support that characterisation. Although Uber's written agreements described Uber as acting merely as a booking agent for the drivers, the Supreme Court in Uber BV v Aslam applied the approach set out in Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher; in other words, the Supreme Court treated the question of worker status as a matter of statutory interpretation rather than contractual interpretation. On that footing, the terms drafted by the putative employer are not the starting point of the analysis. Protective employment legislation exists precisely because the party that drafts such terms usually holds the greater bargaining power, and it cannot be permitted to contract out of statutory rights through careful labelling.

The inquiry therefore turns to the practical realities of control and the allocation of commercial risk. Uber fixed the fares charged to passengers, which indicates that the Uber drivers were subordinate to Uber in the way they performed their services. A driver who cannot negotiate the price of the service he supplies is not running a business of his own in any meaningful sense, because the principal lever by which an independent trader increases earnings has been removed from his hands. The same pattern appears in Uber's control over the terms on which trips are offered, its monitoring of acceptance and cancellation rates, its use of passenger ratings, and its restriction of direct contact between driver and passenger. At least one of two features characteristic of a protected relationship therefore marks the drivers' position, perhaps both: that subordination in the manner of performing the work, or the fact that the Uber drivers were economically dependent on Uber for their work. Either feature, on a purposive reading of the statute, places the individual within the class the legislation was enacted to protect.

As to the statutory category, the Supreme Court classified the Uber drivers as employees under limb (a) of section 230(3) of the Employment Rights Act 1996. It held that the Uber drivers were workers rather than independent contractors, and this holding settles the tension between the booking-agent paperwork and the statutory character of the inquiry. The written description of Uber as a mere intermediary was not disregarded as irrelevant, but it could not displace the conclusion that the statute, read in light of its protective purpose and applied to the facts as they actually operated, brought the drivers within its scope.

The procedural history confirms how contested the issue was at each level. The Court of Appeal dismissed Uber's appeal by a majority in 2018, before the UK Supreme Court handed down its judgment in Uber BV v Aslam on 19 February 2021. The handing down of the judgment on that date led to Lord Leggatt delivering the judgment of the Supreme Court; that is, the Supreme Court's judgment in Uber BV v Aslam was given by Lord Leggatt. His reasoning has since become the principal reference point for tribunals confronting platform work and other arrangements in which documentation and practice diverge.

The composition of the outcome admits only two possibilities. Either all of the Supreme Court Justices who heard Uber BV v Aslam agreed with the result, or at least one Supreme Court Justice dissented in the case; the two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. The Supreme Court's own published judgment records that every Justice who heard the appeal agreed with it, so it is the first of these possibilities that holds. By contrast with that dissenting position, the Supreme Court decided Uber BV v Aslam by a majority of four to one. Whatever the precise division of the bench, the doctrinal lesson is clear: where contract and reality conflict, courts identify the relationship by asking what the statute protects and whether the facts bring the individual within it, treating the written terms as evidence rather than as the determinative answer.
